paper_title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Continual post-training of language models (LMs) is common setting where practitioners aim to inject new capabilities into already-trained models for scenarios such as customizing for specific use-cases and enabling human-like lifelong learning (Shi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Zheng et al., 2025a;b; Srijith et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). Yet, this process is notoriously challenging on both the acquisition (injecting new abilities) and retention (maintaining existing capabilities) axes (Harmon et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b). The failure to retain existing capabilities, widely known as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey & Cohen, 1989; French, 1999; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), is particularly well-documented in settings where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset is used for teacher forcing (Kalajdzievski, 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Shenfeld et al., 2026b). recent work showed that self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) is an effective way to inject SFT demonstrations in an on-policy manner (Shenfeld et al., 2026a), outperforming recent off-policy continual fine-tuning methods such as re-invoke (Lu & Lab, 2025) and Dynamic Fine-tuning (DFT; Wu et al. (2026)) on both acquisition and retention axes. SDFT leverages the in-context learning (ICL) and instruction-following (IF) abilities of post-trained models to provide demonstrations in-context to the self-teacher model, and applies on-policy distillation (OPD; Ross et al. (2011), Agarwal et al. (2024)) on itself, supervising on an implicit self-rewrite of the demonstrations. However, as models struggle with ICL and IF at smaller scales, SDFT remains infeasible in this regime (see Fig. 3a). We aim to address this limitation, as small models have become critical for applications such as on-device deployment, latency-specialized models, draft models, verifiers, and large-small collaborative methods (Cobbe et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Abdin et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Belcak et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026). 1 (a) Averaged across 3 base models, continual posttraining via SYNTHSELF on the medical domain results in near-zero forgetting across all 14 benchmarks. (b) Across 3 base models, 4 acquisition benchmarks, and 14 retention tasks, SYNTHSELF maximizes performance gains with minimal forgetting. Figure 1: Overview of SYNTHSELF performance across three model scales (0.5, 1.5, and 3B). Contribution. To better understand how to leverage the key principles of SDFT, we first examine why it succeeds in continual post-training ( 2.2.1). We reveal that the distribution shift of the posttrained base model linearly correlates with poor acquisition and forgetting  (Fig. 2)  , indicating that staying in-distribution is crucial for continual learning. While the primary advantage of SDFT over off-policy methods is its ability to staying in distribution, evaluating its self-generated offline dataset reveals that SDFTs self-supervision quality is inadequate at smaller model scales  (Fig. 3)  . In response, we propose Synthetic Self-Distillation (SYNTHSELF), which imitates self-distillations implicit in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the distribution-aligned rewrite to larger model ( 2.4). Our method distinctly differs from SDFT in the following ways: (i) choosing off-policy over on-policy supervision allows us to apply rejection sampling, which in turn improves supervision quality for small models that are sensitive to data quality; and (ii) using minimally larger, samefamily aligners allows us to simultaneously (ii.a.) provide high-quality supervision (Tab. 2), (ii.b.) remain in-distribution relative to the base model  (Fig. 4)  , and (ii.c.) maintain low computational costs. We empirically validate SYNTHSELF ( 3), demonstrating that: 1. SYNTHSELF achieves the best acquisition across 3 domains (science, tool-use, and medicine) and 4-subject science mixture while preserving prior capabilities on 14 benchmarks, consistently across 3 base model sizes (0.5, 1.5, 3B), and against 4 relevant baselines (Fig. 1, Tab. 1). 2. Controlling for the confounding factor of teacher model size, we demonstrate that SYNTHSELF outperforms both onand off-policy distillation in acquisition by +5.7%p to +16.9%p, averaged over all four settings and three base scales (Tab. 1, Fig. 5). 3. We show that utilizing smaller (weaker) in-distribution aligner is more effective than deploying larger (stronger) out-of-distribution teacher, yielding 69.9% reduction in alignment computational cost (FLOPs) (Tab. 2). 4. We validate that our improvement over SDFT is not due to prompt differences using prompt-matched and diverse prompts, achieving +18.96%p and +1.68%p gains in acquisition and retention over prompt-matched SDFT  (Fig. 6)  . 5. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that combining rejection sampling with off-policy supervision is meaningful component of our methodology  (Fig. 5)  . 2 (a) ExperFigure 2: Distribution shift negatively correlates with ideal continual learning. iment 1: Post-training distribution shift strongly correlates with forgetting existing capabilities across GPQA-Diamond, ARC-C, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval, and MBPP, regardless of data source or type. Fig. 3a demonstrates that SDFTs performance relative to SFT decreases monotonically with student size. We attribute this to poor self-supervision quality. Further experimental details are in Appendix C. 3.2 RESULTS SYNTHSELF achieves the highest acquisition across all four benchmarks, including the science mixture, while matching the strongest baselines on 14 retention tasks (Tab. 1, Fig. 1). We abbreviate SYNTHSELF as SS, with 1 and 2 denoting aligners one and two sizes larger, respectively (i.e., Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B). Interestingly, recent methods fail to surpass SFT in acquisition at these smaller scales. DFTs performance in the medical domain deteriorates especially significantly; we have double-checked that these evaluation values are correct. However, consistent with the discussion in 2.2.1, the on-policy and in-distribution mechanisms of SDFT and ASFT successfully improve retention over SFT. Moreover, we validate that the performance gains of SYNTHSELF stem primarily from indistribution demonstration injection, rather than merely leveraging larger aligner (Tab. 1). Offand on-policy distillation (Off-/On-PD) use the identical aligner, differing only in conditioning on xi rather than on rewrite(xi, yi). Averaged across all four settings, SYNTHSELF nonetheless improves acquisition by +5.7%p to +16.9%p while maintaining comparable retention. As expected, demonstration injection drives these acquisition gains, whereas all three methods (SYNTHSELF, Off-PD, and On-PD) similarly preserve the base model distribution to sustain retention capabilities. Lastly, we observe that SYNTHSELF does not yield significant improvements over Off-/On-PD in the medical domain. This is likely due to the aligner models already having perfect knowledge of the training data, making demonstration injection largely redundant. Despite this, SYNTHSELF remains highly competitive, successfully outperforming all remaining baselines. 3.3 FURTHER EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSES Distribution matching outweighs aligner capability, and leads to data generation cost savings. We validate our hypothesis that lower-cost, in-distribution aligners are more effective than stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) alternatives. We hypothesize such filtering is especially critical for smaller base models, which are highly sensitive to noisy supervision.

sections.title: 4 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Additional related work. Huang et al. (2026) highlights the impact of distribution drift in SFT using code-generation data on Qwen3-8B. However, they do not directly address continual learning or small language models, restricting their evaluation to limited scales and domains. Furthermore, Li et al. (2026) combines mechanisms that we instead isolate: SDFT-style self-rewrites with similarity filtering, cross-family fusion, and an on-policy KL regularizer; covered individually by our SDFT, on-policy distillation, and ASFT baselines. Crucially, we differ in the supervision source. Because their rewrites originate from the student, they inherit the small-scale degradation shown in Fig. 3. Our same-family aligner explicitly resolves this limitation. Training compute savings and further performance headroom. Rejection sampling reduces training compute by shrinking the dataset ˆD (e.g., by 17.1% for tool use; Tab. 2). Despite training on fewer demonstrations than SFT, SYNTHSELF improves acquisition by +4.2%p on average, proving these gains stem from supervision quality rather than quantity. To further boost performance, practitioners can scale in pass@k, trading inference compute for larger coverage supervision. Limitation and future directions. SYNTHSELF requires larger, same-family aligner. Fortunately, most major open-weight families provide spectrum of model sizes, naturally satisfying this requirement since smaller variants are often distilled from their larger counterparts (e.g., Qwen2.5, Qwen3.5, OLMo 2 (Walsh et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma 4). Nevertheless, future work could explore adapting out-of-family aligners to produce in-distribution supervision. One promising direction is adding the base models answer in-context with an appropriate prompt to generate an in-distribution rewrite.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI to assist with experimental code generation and reviewing writing for grammar and spelling. Furthermore, language models generated the reasoning demonstrations for three SciKnowEval subjects. The Chemistry demonstrations were generated with GPT-4o by Shenfeld et al. (2026a). AI was not used for conceptualization, methodology design, data analysis, or result interpretation. All reported numbers were produced directly by our experimental pipeline, not by language model. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted scripts and text, and we take full responsibility for the final content of this work.
